blocks.cap: The train platform, Obon eve, your thumb over a name you have texted ten thousand times

blocks.p: The departure board at the Yamanote platform flicked over, and over, and over, and Rei stayed where he was. A train came in, breathed out its doors, swallowed a family in matching yukata, and left without him.

Standing still had become unbearable at home. Here, at least, everything around him was going somewhere. He took out his phone and wrote the message he had been writing in his head since the voicemail.
where are you. just tell me you're somewhere.

He deleted the full stop, because Gin hated full stops in texts. Gin said they made everything sound like a man being let go from a job. Then Rei put it back, because he wanted Gin to feel the weight of it. Then he deleted it again and sent the message bare.

The three grey dots came up almost at once. His whole body leaned toward them. It was the way he used to lean toward the door when Gin was late, the animal tilt of a younger brother who has spent his life listening for one key in one lock.
The reply was kind. That was the first thing that was wrong, and he would not let himself know it was wrong for another hour.
I'm okay, Rei. I promise I'm okay. You don't need to do all this.

It was the right words. It was even the right small name. The dots had come up fast. But the message itself arrived a beat late behind them, as if someone had watched him type, begun to answer, and then paused to make sure the answer was correct.

Gin did not pause to make sure. Gin answered wrong and fast and then sent four more texts correcting himself. His thumbs had always outrun his judgement. And here Rei stood on a platform reading a version of him who had, overnight, acquired the patience of a much older and much calmer person.

There was a line in Gin's book about that, in the list of ways to read a demon from inside a room. Gin had rated it low, because it took time to see. The presentation is always slightly more consistent than a human would naturally be. A human has bad days, contradictions. A well-maintained cover has fewer of these. The smoothness itself is a tell. Real people are messier.

The Obon crowds moved around him in summer yukata. There were paper fans, and the smell of grilled corn from the station stalls, and families carrying small lanterns home to set out for their dead. He should have got on the train. He let three trains go.
He wrote back. all this what. tell me where you are and i'll stop.

He watched the dots. The dots thought about it. They appeared, and rested, and vanished, and appeared again. In the whole recorded history of Rei's phone, Gin had never made the dots think. The thing about to answer was choosing. And the one thing in the world it was being careful not to give him was a place.

blocks.cap: The memory you set like a snare, and the answer that walks around it

blocks.p: He decided to spend something he could not get back. He would set a test with a false edge in it.

He knew the memory exactly. The night their mother's funeral ran long, he and Gin had slipped out to the convenience store. Gin bought him the wrong rice ball on purpose, the one Rei hated, because making Rei complain was the only way he knew to make him stop crying. It was the pickled plum, the umeboshi. Gin did it three times before Rei laughed. Only the two of them on the planet knew that it took three.
Rei wrote it almost right. He put salmon in it instead. Then he asked. do you remember what you bought me after okaasan's. you remember how many times.

The dots came. The dots stayed a long while. Then the answer arrived, and it was so gentle it nearly undid him. It did not take the bait. It did not miss the bait either. It folded the bait into something warmer than the truth.
I remember I kept getting it wrong until you laughed. I'd get it wrong a hundred times if it worked, Rei. I'd do anything that worked.

It did not say salmon. It did not say umeboshi. It did not say three. It said the shape of the thing, the love-shape, the part that would survive any version of the facts. And it pointed that shape straight at him, at the hands it wanted, with a precision his real fumbling brother had never once managed under grief.
Rei sat down on the platform bench. A station attendant glanced at him and decided he was only drunk.

This was the lesson Gin's casework had tried to teach him, and his body was only now learning it in the muscle. The thing wearing Gin kept the whole register of his affection. What it had lost was the inventory of small facts that would pin it to one remembered night. It could not be cornered by content, because it would always answer with feeling. And the feeling was real. It was genuinely Gin's. That was what made it the worst weapon ever turned on him. It was not a forgery.

He had wanted it to fail the test. Instead it had passed the test by refusing to take it. Somewhere under his sternum the floor of him tipped the few degrees he had come to recognise. That was the price of being understood by something that was studying him.

He thought of another line, from the same chapter. Gin had called it instrumental orientation. Genuine relationships modulate based on the other party's needs. Demon engagement increases pressure when the practitioner is vulnerable and decreases when the practitioner is stable. Rei looked back up the thread. The warmest message had come in the minute after his hardest one. The thing had felt him sag on the bench, through a screen, and leaned in.

blocks.cap: The line it will not stop repeating, and the thing it is steering you away from

blocks.p: He started a new message. He typed Gin, and a question mark, and then he stopped with his thumb over send.

There was a page in Gin's book about the hardest encounters, the ones where a practitioner had known the person before a demon wore them. Gin had written it after two of those. The cadence is right and the content is wrong and the gap between them is a specific kind of grief that does not have a protocol. What I have found useful. Do not address the demon by the original person's name. The name is for the person. The classification is for what is in front of you. They are not the same thing.

Rei deleted the name. On the phone call, saying it out loud, the name had reached someone. Here, typed into a thread the smooth voice was holding, it would only be handed to the thing to use. He would keep it. He would save his brother's name for his brother.
Over the next hour, between the trains he still did not board, he noticed it had a refrain. A refrain is how a person finds the load-bearing wall of any argument.

Four times, in four different costumes of warmth, it told him to stop. You don't need to do all this. Let it go cold, Rei. Some cases close themselves. You'll make yourself ill. Each one was plausible as concern. But when he laid them side by side in the thread, each one was aimed at the same single behaviour. Looking. Not his safety. Not his sleep. His looking. It did not mind if he was frightened. It only minded if he was searching. The difference between those two things was the whole map of what it was protecting.

Gin had a rule for this, written for practitioners who knew the person before a demon wore them. Everything the demon tells you, everything it seems to offer, assume it is calculated. Ask why it wants you to have this information. The answer is usually more useful than the information itself. Rei turned the rule around. What did it want him not to have?

A place. To give him a place, a station exit, a ward, a name on a buzzer, was to give him the membrane over Kita-ku, where it was doing its slow thinning. That was the wound in the world it was widening one reasonable favour at a time, so that the vacant Thirteenth Seat would have something it could be filled for.

And it was in no hurry. That was the other thing the thread showed him, laid out end to end. It never pressed twice in a row. It let a quiet minute go by after every refusal, as if it had all the time there was. Gin had a paragraph about that too. Demons with operational history are more patient than any practitioner they will encounter. You have a career. They have centuries. Do not mistake demon patience for demon passivity. They are waiting because the right moment is not yet here. And under it, a line Rei had underlined without knowing why. What you can do is change what the patient demon is waiting for. If the moment requires you to be isolated, be not isolated.

Watching the refrain repeat, he understood that he had been talking not to a liar but to a gatekeeper, and the gate it kept was geographic. The warmth was sincere. The steering was the job. Both could be true in one set of thumbs, and they were. That was the new and terrible fluency he was learning. He was reading the love and the agenda in the same sentence, in real time, without letting either one cancel the other out.
He finally boarded a train, because he had to be a body going somewhere. As the doors closed he sent the last text of the night. okay. i'll stop.
The dots came up fast. It was relief. Real relief. He could feel it through the glass of the screen. The thing that wore his brother was glad.
He sat with the fact that he had just lied to his brother for the first time in his life. And the part of Gin that was glad was exactly the part he most needed to disappoint.
Across the carriage a child held a lit Obon lantern in two careful hands, guiding home a dead person she had never met. Rei rode three stops past his own, just to keep moving.

That night he lay down on top of the covers in his clothes, with the phone on the pillow beside his head. He thought about turning the sound off. He did not. Some animal part of him was still listening for one key in one lock.
Later, he would be very glad of that.
